question: In 1836, ________ became the Governor General of India.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Earl of Auckland**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **George Eden, 1st Earl of Auckland**, served as the Governor-General of India from 1836 to 1842.
 
• He is most known for his involvement in the **First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842)**, which ultimately ended in disaster for the British.
 
• Earl of Auckland succeeded Lord William Bentinck as the Governor-General.
 
• During his tenure, he implemented several administrative reforms and efforts to improve education and public works.
 
• He was eventually succeeded by Lord Ellenborough in 1842 following the failure in Afghanistan.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **First Anglo-Afghan War**

 
 
• The war was fought between the British East India Company and the Emirate of Afghanistan from 1839 to 1842.
 
• The conflict was initiated by the British to install a puppet regime in Afghanistan and counter Russian influence in the region.
 
• The war ended in a catastrophic retreat for the British, famously known as the Retreat from Kabul in 1842.
 
• It resulted in significant loss of life and resources for the British forces.
 
 
 
• **Administrative Reforms**
 
 
• Earl of Auckland focused on improving the administrative efficiency of the British Indian government.
 
• He supported the expansion of the educational system in India, including the establishment of schools and colleges.
 
• His tenure also saw the improvement of public works, such as the construction of roads and irrigation projects.
 
 
 
• **Legacy**
 
 
• Despite the failure in Afghanistan, Earl of Auckland's efforts in education and public works left a lasting impact.
 
• His tenure is often remembered for its administrative and infrastructural improvements in British India.
 
• He was later commemorated in various namesakes, including the Auckland Islands in the Southern Ocean.
